Find the wire's push on the bead first; the bead's push on the wire is its equal and
opposite partner.
**Step 1 — set up the angle.** Let the quarter circle have radius R and centre O at the
corner. Measure θ from OA, the **vertical** radius, so the bead starts at θ = 0 and ends
at B with θ = 90°.
**Step 2 — find the speed at angle θ.** The bead has descended a height R(1 − cos θ), and
the wire is frictionless, so
v² = 2gR(1 − cos θ)
**Step 3 — write the radial equation.** Let N be the wire's push on the bead, taken
**inward** (towards O). The inward component of gravity is mg cos θ, and together they
supply the centripetal force:
N + mg cos θ = mv²/R
**Step 4 — substitute v².**
N = 2mg(1 − cos θ) − mg cos θ
**N = mg(2 − 3 cos θ)**
**Step 5 — read the sign.** The sign of N changes where cos θ = 2/3:
**near A** (cos θ ≈ 1): N = −mg, **negative**, so the wire actually pushes the bead
**outward** ✓
**near B** (θ = 90°, cos θ = 0): N = +2mg, **positive**, so the wire pushes the bead
**inward** ✓
**Step 6 — apply Newton's third law.** The bead pushes the wire the **opposite** way:
at the start, **radially inwards**
later, **radially outwards** ✓
**Why it must start that way.** At A the bead is almost at rest, so almost **no**
centripetal force is needed - but gravity already has a full inward component mg ✓ The
wire must push outward to cancel the excess. Lower down the bead is fast, the centripetal
demand mv²/R is large, and the wire must help by pulling it inward.
**Where the switch happens.** N = 0 at cos θ = 2/3, that is **θ = 48·2°** ✓ At that one
instant the bead presses on the wire not at all; a bead on a loose track would leave it
there, which is exactly the condition that governs a ball rolling off a dome.
**Why a bead and not a ball on a track.** The hole lets the wire push **either** way ✓ A
ball resting on a surface could only be pushed outward and would fly off at 48·2°. The
bead is threaded, so it is held on and the force simply reverses.
**Reading the distractors.** **Always outwards** and **always inwards** ✗ both ignore the
sign change in mg(2 − 3 cos θ). **Outwards initially, inwards later** ✗ is the right
physics applied to the wrong body - that describes the force **on the bead**, while the
question asks for the force **on the wire** ✓ The third law reverses it.
∴ radially inwards initially and radially outwards later.

"Just completes" the loop fixes the speed at the top; energy conservation then fixes the
starting height.
**Step 1 — note the radius.** The diameter is D, so
**r = D/2**
**Step 2 — find the minimum speed at the top of the loop.** "Just completes" means the
track exerts **no** force at the highest point B, so gravity alone bends the body into
the circle:
mg = mv_B²/r
**v_B² = gr**
**Step 3 — conserve energy** from the release point (at rest, height h) to the top of the
loop (height 2r, speed v_B). The track is frictionless, so no energy is lost:
mgh = mg(2r) + ½mv_B²
**Step 4 — substitute v_B² = gr and cancel m and g.**
h = 2r + r/2
**h = 5r/2**
**Step 5 — express in terms of D.**
h = (5/2)(D/2)
= **5D/4** ✓
**Why h must exceed the loop's height.** Coasting to the top with **zero** speed would
need only h = 2r = D - but a body creeping over the top falls away from the track instead
of following it ✓ The extra r/2 = D/4 is exactly the kinetic energy that keeps it pressed
to the circle.
**A numerical instance.** With D = 4 m (so r = 2 m) and g = 10 m s⁻²:
v_B² = 20, giving v_B = **4·47 m s⁻¹** at the top
h = 5(4)/4 = **5 m**
check, per kilogram: start 10(5) = **50 J**; at the top 10(4) + ½(20) = 40 + 10 =
**50 J** ✓ energy balances.
**The speed at the bottom.** v_A² = 2gh = 5gr, so v_A = √(5gr) - exactly √5 times the
speed at the top, the standard result for a vertical loop ✓
**Reading the distractors.** **D** ✗ is the bare height of the loop, forgetting the
kinetic energy needed at the top. **3D/2** ✗ overshoots, and **7D/5** ✗ corresponds to no
condition in the problem ✓ The answer must be a little more than D, and only 5D/4 is.
∴ h = 5D/4.

The wire breaks where the **tension** is greatest, so locate the maximum of T around the
vertical circle.
**Step 1 — write the tension at a general point.** Let the wire make angle φ with the
**downward** vertical. Along the wire, towards the centre:
T − mg cos φ = mv²/r
**T = mv²/r + mg cos φ**
**Step 2 — see that both terms peak together.**
**cos φ** is greatest, equal to 1, at the **lowest** point
**v** is greatest at the lowest point too, since that is where the mass has fallen
furthest and energy conservation gives it the most kinetic energy ✓
So the two contributions reach their maxima at the same place, and the tension is
unambiguously largest at the **bottom** ✓
**Step 3 — quantify the difference.** Over the height 2r, energy conservation gives
v_b² = v_t² + 4gr, so
T_bottom − T_top = m(v_b² − v_t²)/r + 2mg
= 4mg + 2mg
= **6mg**
whatever the speed of rotation ✓ The gap never closes, so the bottom is always the weak
point.
**The physical reading.** At the lowest point the wire must **support the weight** and
**turn the fastest-moving part of the motion** at the same time. At the top, gravity
itself provides part of the centripetal force, so the wire is relieved of it ✓
**A worked instance.** For the slowest circle that still works, v_t² = gr:
T_top = m(gr)/r − mg = **0**
T_bottom = 6mg
The wire carries **six times** the weight at the bottom and nothing at the top ✓
**Reading the distractors.** **Highest point** ✗ is where the tension is **least** - the
exact opposite, and the commonest wrong answer because that is where the motion feels
most precarious. **Wire horizontal** ✗ gives T = mv²/r, an intermediate value with cos φ
= 0. **60° from vertical** ✗ is likewise intermediate ✓ T falls smoothly and continuously
from bottom to top, so no interior point can be the maximum.
∴ when the mass is at the lowest point.
